author: Jenny Brown
title: Labor Mobilized for ‘Many vs. Mighty’ Midterms
content:
Something different was in the air as the labor movement mobilized for the midterms.




More than usual, unions were willing to support insurgent candidates who refused corporate donations and bucked the Democratic Party establishment. They championed a Bernie Sanders-style list of working-class issues: Medicare for All, a higher minimum wage, union rights, immigrant rights, stopping war, and taxing the rich. Many are union members themselves. And they won.




United Auto Workers President Shawn Fain called the election “the many versus the mighty.”




In Michigan, the UAW was a key backer of the victorious Abdul El-Sayed, who earlier defeated the party’s depressing primary choice for U.S. Senate.  “You had a lot of rich people who tried to… buy a seat, to buy these races,” Fain told 

Michigan Advance

. “Michiganders… are telling these people they’re not for sale.”




Logger and union member Troy Jackson won a Senate seat against 30-year incumbent Republican Susan Collins in Maine after the UAW and the Maine AFL-CIO helped defeat the establishment choice in the primary there. In Ohio, labor stalwart Sherrod Brown faced a river of crypto lobby cash but recovered the Senate seat he lost in 2024.




In Texas, the Communications Workers (CWA) mobilized for union-member candidates up and down the ticket, asking candidates to commit to a 

“Contract with Working Texans.”

 Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa signed on—she’s a labor lawyer, member of Texas State Employees Union/CWA, and the first Democrat elected Texas governor since 1990.




Various union members and leaders are headed for Congress. Ironworker Brian Poindexter won in Ohio. Pennsylvanians elected firefighter and union president Bob Brooks. Forest Service smokejumper and local union vice president Sam Forstag won in Montana. VA nurse and union member Mitchell Berman beat a Republican incumbent in Wisconsin. 




In New York, UAW members and Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) congressional candidates Claire Valdez and Darializa Avila Chevalier defeated establishment Democrats in the primary, then romped November 3.




Richard Ojeda, a champion of the West Virginia teachers’ strike of 2018, won a Congressional seat in North Carolina, beating the head of the National Republican Congressional Committee. "We were elected to elevate the lives of working people across this country,” 

said Ojeda

. “We're coming in LASER FOCUSED on the mission. Help people. Hold anyone who has hurt people accountable. Tax the billionaires. The end.”




Others lost, but came way closer than expected. In Nebraska, Kellogg’s strike leader and independent Dan Osborn came up short (44-50) for U.S. Senate. He faced ferocious attack ads, with $24 million in ‘independent’ spending. In Florida, former SEIU organizer and DSA member Angie Nixon defeated the establishment Democrat in the primary and almost won (48-50) a Senate race the pundits had written off. She got zero support from the national Democratic Party.




CORPORATE DEMS UNDER FIRE




Now some unions have come out swinging, demanding more from the party. The Machinists (IAM) sent a letter 

urging Senator Chuck Schumer to resign as party leader

. OPEIU 

did the same

.




The IAM “is through with any member of leadership, in any political party, who stops one iota short of being a ferocious, unyielding and unbending champion of working people,” said President Brian Bryant. “This means… sweeping economic policy changes that will recalibrate the vast, immoral, economic injustice in this country.” 




The United Electrical Workers concurred: “The credit for these wins belongs not to the Democratic Party—whose leadership has offered at best tepid resistance to the Republican agenda over the past two years—but to the working people across the country who have spent the last two years organizing and fighting back in their communities and workplaces.”  




UE set out an ambitious agenda

: a $25 minimum wage, Medicare for All, dismantling ICE, taxing the rich, protecting Social Security, and passing labor law reform including the PRO Act and card-check recognition for speedier union recognition. National Nurses United said voters expect a stop to health care cuts, stat. 




President Trump can veto most bills Congress passes, but Vermont Senator Bernie Sanders 

insisted

 on November 9 that Congress needs to do its job and pass a bold working-class agenda. If Trump vetoes the bills, that’ll raise the stakes in 2028 to elect a president who will sign them.




It’ll take a lot of pressure get corporate Democrats to defy their paymasters. So plans are afoot for 

May Day 2028

, when the Auto Workers and other unions have important contracts expiring. The plan is to keep the focus on working class demands, backed by a season of contract campaigns and strikes.

author: Jenny Brown
title: ‘Delay, Deny, Discipline’ Is Amazon’s Real Pregnancy Policy, Workers Say
content:
Willamina Barclay was working as a picker at Amazon’s fulfillment center in Rochester, New York, when she felt lightheaded again. “She pleaded with a manager for a seat… He refused: ‘No, because you don’t have a [pregnancy] accommodation. If I give you a chair, I have to give everybody else a chair,’” he said, according to a recent lawsuit.




But Barclay, who learned she was pregnant in March 2025, had already asked managers many times for accommodations—a seat, extra breaks to drink, eat, pee (or throw up) in the bathroom, no ladder-climbing or squatting, and no heavy lifting.




Amazon—a company known for fast delivery—had failed to answer for weeks, demanding medical documentation. Even after Barclay provided it, Amazon still refused most accommodations, permitting her four breaks a day, but no chair. She was moved to a different position, but still required to lift heavy packages. 




Amazon counted her new breaks against her unpaid time off (UPT), a leave bank that workers accumulate at five minutes per hour and that maxes out at 80 hours. She went to Human Resources several times to try to rectify the situation, but stopped because they were also counting those visits as UPT, the lawsuit says.




The heavy lifting led to sharp pains. At one point she left the warehouse in a wheelchair headed for the hospital. Amazon also counted that time against her unpaid leave bank. On another occasion, she had to leave due to uncontrolled vomiting. Despite a doctor’s note, that was also counted against her. Her UPT thus used up, Amazon fired her.




Under the law, workers cannot be penalized for taking pregnancy-related leave 

(see box at end of article)

.




Barclay’s ordeal is detailed in a lawsuit filed September 8 by 

A Better Balance

, a nonprofit focused on work policies affecting families. It’s a proposed class action on behalf of all U.S. workers whose rights under the Pregnant Workers Fairness Act (PWFA) have been violated by Amazon.




SYSTEMATIC VIOLATIONS




Barclay’s harrowing experience is common, said Sultana Hossain, recording secretary of the Amazon Labor Union (ALU) on Staten Island: Under the law “pregnant workers don’t have to give in paperwork,” she said. “They only have to verbally say, ‘I’m pregnant and I need to be accommodated.’ But we’re seeing Amazon systemically violate that.




“Even if workers get an accommodation eventually, it can take several weeks,” said Hossain. “So people really don’t have any choice but to keep working in their regular role, which is really dangerous if they actually need an accommodation.”




Key’Asia, a worker at Amazon’s fulfillment center near Wilmington, Delaware, said that Amazon management twice rejected a note from her doctor, once because it had an e-signature, and then again when she got an ink signature. (For privacy to discuss medical matters, some workers asked that last names not be used.)




Managers said the signature looked fraudulent and still refused to accommodate her pregnancy, Key’Asia said. “They are making you do the things that your doctor told you that you’re not supposed to be doing,” she told attendees at an online Jobs With Justice event in October. “They’re making you do things that are putting yourself and your baby at risk.” She said Amazon fired her twice, both times when she was pregnant.




PATTERN OF ILLEGALITY




Workers have noticed a pattern: When they request accommodations, Amazon managers ask if they are “safe to work.” If they say “yes,” they are forced to continue to work without accommodations. If they say “no,” Amazon puts them on 

unpaid leave

, which rapidly runs out.




Marissa, who worked at Amazon’s fulfillment center in Rossford, Ohio, said that after her accommodations were denied, she was forced out on unpaid leave, and she ended up losing her apartment. “I was out $1,700… I couldn’t pay for my vehicle. I couldn’t afford to eat.




“Amazon doesn’t care about whether or not you’re in pain,” she said. “They care about whether or not you can get their packages out on time.”




Hossain said it was typical for workers to get fired for “job abandonment” because “they ran out of time-off options because they were just not given the accommodation.” (A Better Balance 

has also sued

 Amazon for this practice on behalf of a disabled worker.)




TRAGIC RESULTS




Hayat Bzezi was working at Amazon’s Staten Island JFK8 warehouse during the busy holiday season of 2024, when all workers were required to take an additional weekly 10-hour shift. She had asked for lighter duty, and management said she could use a chair, but then she was denied it. 




She was “lifting heavy products, climbing up and down the stairs, despite having a high-risk pregnancy,” said her husband Wajdy, an elected ALU trustee who works at the same warehouse.




Hayat worked through pain, but it got worse and finally she had to go to the hospital, where she miscarried. It was the second time she had miscarried while working at Amazon. After that the couple decided to 

speak out

. Since then, she has stopped working at Amazon and has been able to bear a child.




LAW REDUCES MISCARRIAGES




When the PWFA went into effect in 2023, 

a study found

 that it reduced miscarriages by 9.6 percent. This suggests that many more miscarriages could be avoided if Amazon, the country’s second-largest private employer, started following the law.










 Pregnant 

With

 A Contract 







Postal workers move packages like Amazon warehouse workers do, but they have a union contract. It makes all the difference when you’re pregnant, said Postal Workers (APWU) national field organizer Lori Cash. 




She hired into a heavy job at the Postal Service in 1998 while pregnant with her third child. After a couple of months, her doctor told her she needed to stop work, but she had no sick leave or vacation time accrued. “I went to my union steward, and I said, ‘This is what my doctor is telling me, I’m scared.’ I had no idea what my rights were. I’d never been in a union before.” 




Her steward explained that she could take leave without pay, under the contract, and could not be fired: “We have a just cause process in our contract. They have to prove that they had a just reason to fire you, and just using too much time off without being paid is not justified.”




After the birth, Cash came back to work, but it was too hard: “I had two toddlers and a newborn. I was trying to go back to work with all those shenanigans going on at my house with all these babies.” She told her steward she was thinking of quitting. But her steward fought for her to get the option to come back with fewer hours and gradually increase them, which was also guaranteed in their contract.




“Pregnancy is stressful,” said Cash. “You have so much to worry about.” But during her next pregnancy, she felt “much more confident that I was going to be able to get the accommodations I needed. I had a whole union behind me, fighting to make sure that those rights were given to me, and to make sure that I had a healthy pregnancy and was able to take the time that I needed for me, and for my baby to be taken care of.”





But there is every indication that Amazon is ignoring it. Last year, New Jersey’s attorney general 

filed a lawsuit

 against Amazon after reviewing thousands of worker requests for accommodations. Amazon is New Jersey’s largest private employer, with around 50,000 workers.




“When Amazon’s pregnant workers and workers with disabilities request accommodations, Amazon stonewalls them,” the suit charges. “It forces them through a byzantine accommodations process, imposing rigid and unnecessary paperwork requirements and subjecting workers to unexplained weeks-long delays.”




Rosa, a worker at Amazon’s fulfillment center in Akron, Ohio, said she asked for pregnancy accommodations because she was working in Ship Dock, a role that requires heavy lifting, pushing, and pulling. She was hospitalized for dehydration four times, but managers still kept her in that role, she said.




“Eventually my symptoms became so severe that I had to take an unpaid leave of absence,” she said. “I found out afterwards that I could have done paid short-term disability leave, but these options weren’t told to me.”




Amazon denies this. “The suggestion that we routinely deny or don’t support pregnancy accommodations is simply untrue,” said Amazon spokesperson Kelly Nantel. She said “99.9 percent” of pregnancy accommodation requests this year had been approved.




But New Jersey investigators found that Amazon regularly fired workers for requesting accommodations, in violation of New Jersey’s Law Against Discrimination and the PWFA. New York State 

has also sued

 Amazon for this.




Hossain said the medical forms that Amazon requires for pregnancy, injury, and disability accommodations are so comprehensive and invasive that doctors have objected that they violate medical privacy laws.




Amazon wants such detailed medical documentation, Hossain said, because “they want to claim that if workers ever get injured, it’s because of conditions they came to work with, and it’s not workplace injuries.” Asked about this, an Amazon public relations representative declined to respond.




PACE DRIVES INJURIES




The worker justice group 

Warehouse Life

 has been tracking and protesting Amazon’s health and safety record since 2023, and helping injured workers who have to “fight through a lot of misinformation and lies that they received from [Amazon] managers about workers’ comp,” said Chloe Sigal, campaign manager for the group.




Sigal said Amazon’s rate system, along with “time off task” (TOT) policies, make the work unsafe: “Amazon is pushing people to work as fast, as hard as humanly possible—or really outside what is humanly possible. That’s what’s driving this 

injury epidemic

.”




In 2021 the California legislature found that injuries in Amazon warehouses were driven by its rate system. Workers were forced to work faster and faster because if they fell into the lowest 25 percent they could experience discipline, and the bottom 5 percent risked termination.




California passed a law requiring warehouses to publish stable quotas and not constantly accelerate them. In 2024 the state 

fined

 Amazon $6 million for violating it. 




Workers also accumulate TOT when surveillance detects a pause in their package scanning. Fear of too much TOT pushes workers to cut short their breaks, skip bathroom breaks (and reduce liquid consumption to match), and push on through pain. Dehydration is particularly risky during a pregnancy. “The reason that people are miscarrying at Amazon is because of this rate system,” said Sigal.




Doctors agree. Jenny Fish is a Santa Rosa, California, physician who provides prenatal care. “Prolonged standing, going the whole shift without water, lifting more than 15 to 20 pounds, working night shifts regularly,” she said, “all of this has been irrefutably linked to higher risk of miscarriage, preeclampsia, increased maternal fatigue, preterm delivery, low birth weight, and just in general adverse birth outcomes.” Preeclampsia is potentially fatal.




IS THERE A POLICY?




Sigal said that soon after Warehouse Life started, several Amazon workers came to the group reporting pregnancy issues. But when the group put out a call on social media for experiences working at Amazon while pregnant, it was flooded with stories. Two thousand women from 40 states responded, and 81 described loss of a pregnancy. (To talk to Warehouse Life, 

schedule a call here

.)




Now some of these workers are leading the charge to get changes at the company. They have put pressure on New York City’s Mt. Sinai Health System to terminate Amazon Board of Directors member Edith Cooper as a hospital trustee, given Amazon’s dismal safety record.




Warehouse Life members have also met with Amazon management. Sigal said that during those meetings Amazon claimed to have a policy on pregnancy that was only available to workers. But no workers were able to access it. “Nobody has it. We’ve heard from managers that they don’t have it either, that they don’t receive training on what to do,” Sigal said.




When Labor Notes asked Amazon for its pregnancy policy and any training materials, no documents were forthcoming. Warehouse Life counters that the company’s real pregnancy policy is 

“Delay. Deny. Discipline.”




MARCH ON H.R.




The Amazon Labor Union organized on Staten Island in 2022, and in 2024 affiliated with the Teamsters. But Amazon refuses to negotiate with the union at the 5,000-worker warehouse, despite being ordered to do so by the National Labor Relations Board in April.




The union can still help, though. “Just a few weeks ago a pregnant worker came to our union hall saying she wanted help getting an accommodation at work,” said ALU’s Hossain. The worker had already told her manager that she was pregnant.




The union sent several workers to accompany her to H.R., saying “that should be enough, and Amazon needs to start the process of accommodating her,” Hossain said. “And they actually did listen, but only because a group of workers accompanied her.” A contract could provide additional protections 

(see box at upper right)

.




The union isn’t waiting for workers to seek it out. Union activists distribute fliers with a QR code to a reporting form that goes to the union. Half of the reports “are unfair discipline, the other half is workers who are dealing with injuries or the accommodation process or need workers’ comp or whatever,” said Hossain. “It’s such a big issue.” 




“It really does feel like we’re all just numbers,” said Rosa in Akron. “I want them to take more accountability. They make it so hard when it comes to a life-changing thing.”			     










 Pregnancy Rights 







It has been illegal to discriminate against pregnant workers since 1978, when feminist agitation won the 

Pregnancy Discrimination Act

 (under Title VII of the 1964 Civil Rights Act), which says employers can’t discriminate based on pregnancy, childbirth, or related medical conditions. Before that, many employers had a policy of terminating workers when they got pregnant, and pregnant women often weren’t eligible for unemployment insurance.




In 2023, the 

Pregnant Workers Fairness Act

 strengthened pregnancy rights. Now employers are required to make reasonable accommodations.




The Equal Employment Opportunity Commission has found that reasonable accommodations which don’t require a doctor’s note include: a seat; additional breaks to eat, drink, or use the bathroom; adjusted uniforms and safety equipment; and changes to your job duties or your schedule to make it possible for you to keep working safely while you’re pregnant or recovering from a birth.




Additional accommodations that might require a doctor’s note include limits on weight you have to lift, bending, and ladder use. “But you still have the right to get those accommodations quickly and have them implemented effectively,” said Katherine Greenberg, attorney with 

A Better Balance

. 




“It is illegal for employers like Amazon to force workers to take a leave of absence if there’s an on-the-job accommodation that would keep them safe and allow them to keep working and earning an income,” said Greenberg. Also, employers can’t punish workers for asking for or needing accommodations.




“If you need to pump milk for your baby, you have the right to take a lactation break without being punished for too much time off task,” said Greenberg. “Or if you experience a miscarriage and you need to miss work to recover, you have the right to take that time without being deducted UPT or assigned points for your absence.”




Your state or city may have additional protections; 

check here

. Have a question or concern about your pregnancy at Amazon? 

Schedule a call with Warehouse Life here

.

author: Labor Notes Staff
title: Stewards Corner: Laying the Foundation for Change in Your Union
content:
Revitalizing a local union may require electing new officers with a different vision. But running for office should not be your first step.




Successful campaigns for union office usually start by organizing against management first, often years in advance of any eventual run.




A group of workers wants to accomplish something—better pay, more control over their conditions on the job, an end to tiered wages or benefits—but their officials, or something about the way their union operates, is in the way. So they begin to change the culture of the union, getting more members involved in building power on the shop floor.




Your ultimate goal, after all, is not just electing new leaders, but building a stronger union. And doing that means involving as many members as possible.




WHERE TO START




The good news is you can begin organizing for change in your union any time. 




“Your campaign should start with workplace fights that involve your co-workers,” says John Pearson, a nurse at Highland Hospital in Oakland, California, and former president of the SEIU Local 1021 chapter there. “You need that type of credibility and trust from people to be able to lead successfully.”




Before running for office, Pearson helped lead a campaign to defend breaks, involving nurses throughout the Alameda County hospital system, which resulted in a big back pay settlement. He also led an effort to save a substance abuse clinic from defunding.




“The word spreads if you’re effective at fighting in the workplace—people know to ask you for help,” says Pearson.




This type of organizing shows members that you have a track record, and that collectively members can make a difference.




The Caucus of Rank-and-File Educators (CORE), which won leadership in the Chicago Teachers Union in 2010, built up strength in campaigns like a fight to stop the school district from closing dozens of neighborhood schools and replacing them with privately run charters. 




“So much of our caucus was really forged in the fight against school closings,” says Norine Gutekanst, who was a third-grade teacher at the time. Caucus members attended school closing hearings and teamed up with community activists to camp out all night in front of threatened schools. The leadership of the union, meanwhile, was absent from the fight.




CORE was already “doing what the union should have been doing,” said Chicago social studies teacher Bill Lamme. “So when the election came, [CORE activists] didn’t say ‘Elect me and I’ll do this.’ They said, ‘This is what we’ve been doing and we’ll keep doing it.’”




ATTEND MEETINGS




If you’re serious about getting involved in and transforming your union, you should be regularly attending union meetings, even if the meetings don’t allow for much debate. Bring other members who share your views. By participating, your group can shake things up.




“The first time you attend a meeting, just listen,” says Ken Paff, longtime national organizer with Teamsters for a Democratic Union. 




“Later on,” Paff says, “you can make a proposal, and organize your group to present it. Talk to members before the meeting; draw them in. Get things out to the members, not only to make your group transparent, but also to make union meetings that way.




“Tell people there will be a motion on the pension plan, or another burning topic. Ask them to come support the motion. Put it out in writing. Get them to sign a petition in support of it.”




In Letter Carriers (NALC) Branch 9 in Minneapolis, a group of members started meeting to talk about how to change the culture of their branch, including its meeting agendas. “We had a president of over 30 years who would just use Robert’s Rules to keep people down,” says letter carrier Chris Pennock.




But the group of reformers kept bringing more members to meetings. Eventually their motions started winning. Pennock got 10 minutes on the agenda to talk about fighting post office closures. It was a small step, but a co-worker told him: “I don’t know if you know how historic that is—I’ve never seen a motion pass that the executive board not only didn’t support but were actively opposed to.”




Their organizing helped lay the basis to run a reform slate; Pennock is now vice president of Branch 9. “Have faith that you can change the culture,” he says.




At the same time, “it’s a mistake to think that meetings are the important thing,” says SEIU Local 1021’s Pearson—especially since most members won’t attend meetings. You want to find other ways to get them involved in the union. 




“Talk to people in the workplace, especially while you’re working, if you can,” advises Pearson.  Some other activities to consider:







Holding classes or discussions on issues the union is not addressing




Getting members to join rallies or picket lines in solidarity with other unions




Organizing a “Vote No” campaign on a subpar contract




Campaigning to change your bylaws to make the union more democratic







BE AN INFORMATION SOURCE




Is your local union run like a small club or clique, with a few insiders making all of the decisions and everyone else wondering what’s going on? Do members feel they don’t have a voice in critical decisions about their jobs, benefits, and contracts?




Members want information, and informed members are more active members. You can start building a campaign for change by becoming an information source. Here are some ideas:







Inform members about the contract and how to enforce it




Take on workplace issues and organize contract enforcement campaigns




Organize short gatherings at lunch or after work to talk about workplace or union issues




Distribute bulletins on workplace and union issues




Hold online or in-person workshops or an educational conference




Use an app like WhatsApp to build communication and spread information among members




Start a Facebook group to share news about your employer and give members a space to communicate with each other 




Start an email and text list to send other members news about your local







Don’t spread rumors or conspiracy theories. Be reliable and provide information that the members can use. Set a positive and constructive tone, especially if you’re using social media. 




Remember, your credibility is your most important asset.




GETTING MEMBERS INVOLVED




A one-person crusade isn’t going to change your local union, and it isn’t what the union needs. You need teammates and helpers if you want to accomplish long-term change.




“Every day you need to ask yourself, ‘Who did I talk to today?’” says Vance Smith of Teamsters Local 135 in Indianapolis. “Get out in the field and have one-on-one, personal conversations.”




Have realistic expectations. Not every member is going to want to become as active as you are.




If someone wants to get involved, start them off with small jobs first, like talking to you about problems where they work or introducing you to other members. Thank them for their efforts and let them know their work is valuable. 




“In every workplace, workers show a range of knowledge about and interest in the union, from A to Z,” says longtime organizer Joe Fahey. Don’t try to move people from A to Z immediately—instead, move them from A to B, and so on.




Once they’ve gotten their feet wet, ask them to do bigger jobs, like passing out a leaflet or standing with you in the parking lot while you do that. Give them options. 




Remember, people’s lives are complicated. If someone doesn’t want to get involved at first, don’t write them off. Stay in contact and ask them again later. You’re building a network here, so cast as wide a net as you can. People can surprise you.




The more members you have working with you, the more work you can get done. Especially in a local that represents multiple workplaces or industries, getting lots of members involved in your campaign can be critical.	










Is It Working?







Here are some of the ways you can tell your organizing is having an effect:







More members are involved in a passive way, like reading a leaflet.




More members are taking a small action step, like wearing a button or signing a petition.




Some members are taking on organizing tasks, like passing out flyers or making phone calls.




Some members are becoming leaders and taking initiative.







If these things aren’t happening, take a step back and re-evaluate your strategy. Are you doing too much yourself? Do you need to reach out to more departments? Do you have the right message?




This advice is drawn from the Labor Notes book 

Democracy Is Power 

by Mike Parker and Martha Gruelle.







This article is excerpted from 

Running for Local Union Office: A Labor Notes Guide.

 Order the book ($20) and find resources including how to be effective at union meetings, a list of labor education programs, and more at 

labornotes.org/runningforoffice

.

author: Unknown
title: We Started the School Year with a March on the Principal
content:
At Ferndale High School, nestled in a Detroit suburb, one of our most pressing problems is the dilapidated building, built in the 1950s.




The outdated heating and cooling systems are prone to classroom floods—in the last nine months I've experienced three. Once boiling hot water sprayed out of the HVAC unit during class, nearly injuring a student.




It was late August—our last Sunday night of freedom before our teacher professional development week—when six of my co-workers and I received an email from our principal. She said that a few classrooms had flooded again the previous week, but the damage was limited and our classrooms were “ready for our return.”




“Tomorrow is still the beginning of a fresh school year,” she wrote, “and I’m looking forward to welcoming everyone back and starting the year together on a positive note.”




She made the mistake of including all affected teachers as recipients, instead of blind copying us, so I knew exactly who to reach out to. 




That evening I spent lots of time on the phone with my co-workers and my fellow union building representatives. We all had experienced previous flooding, so we were skeptical that our classrooms would 

actually

 be ready for our return the following morning.




Ever since I began working at this school in 2024, my mission has been to convince my co-workers we should be compensated in some way when our school administrators fail us. Whenever we’ve asked administrators to address issues like poor attendance or facilities problems, we’ve gotten responses like “That is not my fault” or “I do not have the power to fix that.” This energy has been so demoralizing for our teaching staff, and it seemed to me that my co-workers had gotten used to just accepting the b.s.




But having cut my teeth as a political organizer on my college campus and read 

Secrets of a Successful Organizer

, I could tell that 

this issue had the juice we needed to lead a workplace action

—everyone cared enough to do something about it. By Monday morning I had 

devised a plan

 with the support of my fellow building reps.




INDUSTRIAL FANS




Our suspicions were correct; words can hardly describe the scene we walked into. Each of the seven flooded classrooms had eight to 15 industrial fans blowing on the floor, dehumidifying machines siphoning water out of the classroom windows, and no functioning air conditioning.




Teachers were supposed to spend this day organizing and preparing our classrooms. Most of us spend hundreds of dollars of our own money to purchase supplies, decor, soft lighting, and small comforting touches to make our classrooms the warm, safe environments we know students need. It takes a fair amount of time to unpack those things from the summer months and get the space ready for the school year. 




When I saw the state of my classroom, I knew it was going to be impossible to get any sort of work done in that environment. My next step was to walk door to door and check in on my six co-workers who had been looped in on that email. No classroom was even close to being a functional workspace.




I could feel the swelling anger, and knew the moment was ripe to make an ask. “We do not deserve this,” I told my co-workers. “What if we all went to the principal and asked for something in return?”




I told them about the plan the other building reps and I had come up with: The affected teachers could march together to the principal’s office and ask that either we receive pay for the additional hours it takes us to set up our classrooms outside of contract time, or we be excused from a professional development session during the week to set up our classrooms during work hours. 




Everyone was too angry to be afraid. All but one agreed to join our march on the boss. 




The six of us found our principal in a teacher’s classroom. She stepped into the hall to see us standing there shoulder to shoulder, looking upset. None of us will ever forget her response: She took out her phone, started filming us, and said, “Oh I am going to put this on TikTok, it’s the first day of school and the teachers already want something from me.”




When she saw how deeply stunned we were, she put her phone back in her pocket and asked what was wrong. I reminded her of her email, and informed her that our classrooms were in fact not “ready for our return.”




I told her this wasn’t fair to us, and explained how we felt it could be rectified. She said she understood our frustration and would “look into” allowing us to timecard extra hours.




We did not feel incredibly hopeful. There’s too much wiggle room in the phrase “I will look into that.” But to our surprise, we received an email from the principal saying she would be able to approve three hours of paid time for classroom setup.




LESSONS LEARNED




Since this action, I have debriefed with the teachers that participated. While we’re glad we won some compensation, we realized we should have come with a number in mind. We were doubtful that we would win any kind of concession, so we didn’t even think that far ahead. We were able to get the most necessary work done within the three approved hours, but could have benefited from more time.




Still, once the rest of our staff heard about our action, our building was buzzing with excitement. I heard co-workers 15 to 25 years my senior say, “That was so cool!” “I didn’t even know you could do that!” “I wish I was as brave as you when I was your age!” So in my mind, it was a success.




I think the most powerful thing we can do as organizers is be hopeful, and share that hope. The message of “You do not deserve this mistreatment” seemed to really resonate. In education, we grow so used to getting beat down from all angles that we can forget we deserve to be treated with dignity.




I’m very proud to have helped my co-workers work together at that moment. I hope this will help us find the courage to take on our next workplace issue without fear.




Kayla Sharpe is a high school social studies teacher in Ferndale, Michigan, and a building representative with the Ferndale Education Association.

author: Diana Varenik and Natascha Elena Uhlmann
title: Lessons from an 85-Day Hotel Strike
content:
You’d be forgiven for worrying, 12 weeks into a strike, that the boss is hell-bent on waiting you out. But after more than 80 days on the picket line at Seattle’s Embassy Suites by Hilton in Pioneer Square, Aspen Desmarais was undeterred. “I can live on a budget,” she said. “Been doing it since day one.”




After 85 days, on September 10, workers won the longest hotel strike in Washington state history. Their union, UNITE HERE Local 8, represents 4,000 hospitality workers in Oregon and Washington.




Desmarais, a strike captain and bartender at the hotel, worked to keep others motivated throughout the fight. She and her co-workers were “tired of people talking down to us and not treating us with respect,” she said, “when we’re the reason that place stays running the way that it does.”




Hilton’s offer, two weeks into the strike, of 

one cent per hour over its previous proposal

 helped fuel outrage. The union held open bargaining, so members heard the offer firsthand. “I [felt] frustrated and disrespected,” Desmarais said. “Especially with how much hard work my co-workers put into making sure the hotel and its guests have clean spaces and stays that are welcoming.” 




Fritzie Corral, an Embassy Suites breakfast attendant, had only worked at the hotel for two months before walking out. As the strike went on, she said, her son worried that she had made a mistake in taking the job.




“You see other employees that decided to stay in the hotel working," she said. “Even during that time, I still believed I made the right choice. It’s my right to voice out what I feel and to fight for my rights.” 




Hilton did not respond to requests for comment. 




PROTECTION FROM ICE




Workers won significant pay increases, lowered barriers for health care eligibility, and highly sought-after protections for immigrant workers. Hilton, which manages the hotel, drew protests earlier this year for housing ICE agents and for 

cutting ties with

 a Minneapolis hotel that canceled ICE bookings during Operation Metro Surge.




The union’s leaders criticized Hilton throughout the strike for dismissing contract language that would protect immigrant workers. “With ICE-related killings in the news for months causing immigrant workers to worry, why is Hilton refusing to give immigrant workers’ union a heads up if ICE is staying at the hotel?” Local 8 President Anita Seth 

asked 

Businesswire

.




Ultimately workers won a commitment from Hilton not to punish workers who call out due to an immigration enforcement surge, plus language binding the hotel to an expedited resolution process in such an event. Workers who lose their work authorization due to immigration enforcement will now be able to return to their jobs if their work authorization is restored within four years, and retain their seniority for up to two. 




Desmarais told 

Labor Notes

 that making sure immigrant co-workers missing work because of ICE “knew they would have a job still and a safe place to come back to” was the “most important” win strikers fought for.




Starting in 2027, housekeepers will make over $31 an hour—a giant step above the $17.63 an hour that housekeepers make on average across the country, per the Bureau of Labor Statistics. The new contract makes them the highest-paid housekeepers in the state, according to the union. Embassy Suites workers classified as “tipped” will now make $1 more per hour than the city’s minimum wage. 




Health care eligibility was also a core demand for the union. Many hotel workers under collective bargaining agreements must meet a minimum threshold of hours worked to qualify for health benefits in a given period. Seasonal layoffs, a hallmark of hotel work, often mean inconsistent coverage for workers and their families.




The new contract replaces the month-to-month eligibility standard with an annual threshold of 1,250 hours, or around 24 hours a week, to qualify.




MASS CANCELLATIONS




The strike coincided with five of the six World Cup soccer matches held at Seattle’s Lumen Field this summer, directly across from the Embassy Suites. World Cup-related leverage helped produce 

quick contract wins

 this summer for service and hospitality workers in Philadelphia, New York, and Los Angeles, but not so in Seattle. 




How did strikers there keep up the pressure for another 63 days after the games ended? The hotel’s proximity to Lumen Field makes it a destination for football fans when the season starts in September. On game days, the hotel sets up a bar facing the stadium. Workers set up a separate picket line mere feet away from the customers, and urged fans not to cross. 




In between sporting events, Desmarais said solidarity from other union workers played a big role.




Combined pressure from BNSF rail workers (represented by the Brotherhood of Locomotive Engineers and Trainmen Division 518) and sympathetic elected officials pushed Sound Transit to move its contract to another hotel with no promise of return. The transit agency had maintained a block of rooms for the BNSF workers who operate its commuter rail—accounting for 25 rooms nightly, or roughly $18,500 in weekly revenues, 

according to Local 8

, and a significant portion of the hotel’s income during low-traffic winter months.




Embassy Suites workers like Desmarais worked hard to push Sound Transit and other hotel clients to honor the picket line. “There was one day I had to make over 90 phone calls,” she said. “For the most part, it was actually a pretty positive reaction.”




Teamster sanitation and UPS workers also refused to service the hotel during the strike. Corral reported seeing the hotel’s director and assistant director hauling garbage out during the World Cup. “It felt so rewarding,” said Desmarais. “Yeah, you have to get your hands dirty and not just do paperwork. I think it gave them a real experience of what we have to deal with.” 




Corral said community solidarity was key in getting Hilton to concede. Strikers’ church groups joined the picket line. So did several Seattle elected officials and even some hotel guests. Guests also brought workers donuts, contributed to the strike fund, and left Google reviews urging hotel management to “come to the table” and “sign the contract already.”




One temp worker 

walked off the job

 after only an hour to join the picket line. Corral said such displays of solidarity made workers “more motivated to keep on.” 




Many workers worried about money, the future of their jobs, and their families while on strike. But when someone was scared or upset, there was always another worker to help uplift them, said Corral: “We’re like family.”

author: Carlos Pérez
title: “Esto no para”: Una perspectiva de base sobre la huelga indefinida por la educación pública en Madrid
content:
“Esto no para”: Una perspectiva de base sobre la huelga indefinida por la educación pública en Madrid




Desde el 14 de octubre, las docentes de Madrid, España, se encuentran en huelga indefinida en defensa de la educación pública. Tras años de deterioro de las condiciones laborales y una organización sistemática de las bases, las docentes han inundado las calles de la capital española en una movilización masiva que ha vinculado la lucha por la educación pública con la reciente revuelta en torno a la vivienda.




La lucha conjunta por la vivienda y la educación pública en España se encamina ahora hacia una huelga general el 11 de noviembre, en medio de un levantamiento más amplio que se extiende por toda Europa.




Carlos Pérez, maestro de estudios sociales en Carolina del Norte y miembro de la junta directiva de Labor Notes habló con María, profesora de secundaria de historia y geografía en Madrid y militante de Menos Lectivas, una de las principales fuerzas de base detrás de la huelga.




Pérez: Los docentes de la escuela pública en Madrid mantienen una huelga indefinida desde el 14 de octubre. ¿Cuáles son los motivos principales que les llevaron a usted y a otros docentes a convocar una huelga, y cuáles son sus reivindicaciones?




María:

 En la Comunidad de Madrid venimos arrastrando recortes en la educación pública desde el año 2011. Estos han ido deteriorando el estado de las aulas y la calidad educativa de los estudiantes madrileños. 




La falta de recursos y de personal, la cantidad de alumnos en el aula, el aumento de horas lectivas (horas de clase directa en el aula) y la falta de mantenimiento y construcción de infraestructuras nos han dejado un escenario en el que impartir clase es muy complicado. Las docentes no llegamos a atender a todos nuestros estudiantes y hemos decidido plantarnos ante el maltrato institucional que sufrimos tanto nosotras como nuestro alumnado.




En mi caso, he dado clase a aulas de bachillerato con 33 alumnos, he tenido que buscar un aula donde meter a mis alumnos cada día durante un mes de lluvias intensas porque las aulas tenían unas goteras que provocan que estuviesen constantemente mojadas; mis alumnos con necesidades educativas (autismo o dificultades de audición y lenguaje) no han sido atendidos por las profesionales que hacían falta porque no había ni integradora social ni profesora específica para ellos, y por supuesto trabajo una cantidad de horas extra ingentes y no están remuneradas ni reconocidas. 




Por eso reivindicamos y exigimos a la Comunidad de Madrid que reduzca las horas lectivas; reducir los ratios entre las docentes y alumnos; acabar con la segregación, dado que la Comunidad de Madrid es la región de España más segregada en educación; aumentar el salario para equiparlo a las necesidades económicas actuales; reducir la burocracia, entre otras cosas. 




Menos Lectivas, una plataforma de base que agrupa a varios sindicatos, ha sido uno de los principales impulsores de la huelga. ¿Qué es Menos Lectivas y qué papel ha desempeñado en este conflicto?




Menos Lectivas nace en el 2023, inspirada por colectivos como Labor Notes en los EEUU, con la intención de organizar a las trabajadoras de la educación desde los centros de trabajo y devolver el poder sindical a las trabajadoras. Desde entonces hemos construido nuestro movimiento a través de asambleas de centro. 




En estos años previos a la huelga indefinida se han convocado huelgas, manifestaciones y concentraciones que han servido para que cada vez el movimiento fuese más grande y, sobre todo, tuviésemos legitimidad institucional — tanto con los trabajadores que nos ven como un agente de lucha válido porque se sienten parte de él gracias a las asambleas, como para el resto de sindicatos, los medios de comunicación y en última instancia los gobiernos — para decidir cómo, cuándo y dónde queríamos luchar por el derecho a la educación y nuestros derechos laborales.




Desde los inicios sabíamos que la huelga indefinida sería la última herramienta de lucha sindical si nuestras demandas no eran escuchadas por la Comunidad de Madrid y, el pasado junio, se decidió en asamblea que las docentes iríamos a la huelga indefinida. Siendo ya un conjunto de asambleas con legitimidad el resto de sindicatos que no formaban parte de Menos Lectivas tuvieron que sentarse con nosotras en el Comité de Huelga a negociar la constitución de una mesa de negociación y las condiciones de la huelga. Este hito ya es un éxito, consiguiendo que el poder vuelva a las trabajadoras y salga de los despachos.




¿Cómo ha sido recibida la huelga por parte del alumnado y sus familias?




Tanto las familias como el alumnado están de acuerdo con nuestras reivindicaciones. En última instancia, son los principales beneficiarios de las mejoras que consigamos. Nos sentimos muy apoyadas por ellos y son una parte esencial de la lucha.




Los estudiantes organizados han convocado también huelga indefinida a través de distintos partidos y organizaciones políticas como el Sindicato de Estudiantes o la Organización Estudiantil Socialista. Están presentes en todas las acciones que hacemos en las calles y forman una parte importante de la lucha por la educación. 




Las familias, por su parte, se organizan en asociaciones de familias en cada uno de los centros educativos y en los barrios y ayudan a sostener las cajas de resistencia. Además, han convocado una concentración propia para hacerle ver a la Consejera de Educación que esta lucha no es exclusiva de las docentes, si no también de las familias.




Dado que la huelga es indefinida, ¿qué tipo de tácticas han empleado para mantener la participación colectiva y la presión? 




Estamos en la calle constantemente, concentraciones, manifestaciones, performances, asambleas y ocupando el espacio suficiente como para que los medios se hagan eco de nuestras reivindicaciones. 




Es importante que toda la ciudadanía nos vea y nos escuche para que sean conscientes de la realidad de las aulas. En cuanto son conscientes de ella, se unen a la lucha, como mencioné con los estudiantes y sus familias.




Esta huelga tiene lugar bajo el gobierno progresista de Pedro Sánchez, del Partido Socialista Obrero Español (PSOE). ¿Cómo ha respondido el gobierno de Sánchez ante la huelga?




El pasado 5 de octubre el presidente del Gobierno convocó elecciones generales en España, por lo que está huelga ha entrado dentro de su campaña electoral. No les ha quedado otra que mostrar su apoyo a las docentes madrileñas. 




Sin embargo, en los 8 años que el PSOE lleva gobernando en España, no han hecho nada por mejorar las condiciones del profesorado ni del alumnado. Desde el gobierno se limpian las manos y argumentan que las competencias en Educación son de las Comunidades Autónomas pero el Ministerio de Educación y el Gobierno Central son responsables tanto de las condiciones de los trabajadores como de la educación de todos los españoles. 




Además, la Delegación de Gobierno, que pertenece y dirige al Gobierno central y que controla la Policía Nacional, no está dando explicaciones sobre las brutales cargas policiales que hemos sufrido, tanto los docentes como los alumnos, durante las manifestaciones y concentraciones de este último mes.




La huelga en la enseñanza pública coincide con un movimiento masivo en torno a la vivienda, tanto en Madrid como en otros lugares. ¿Hasta qué punto están vinculadas ambas luchas?




Menos Lectivas siempre ha estado muy unida con el Sindicato de Inquilinas de Madrid. Hace un año se empezó a desarrollar el protocolo “Sin vivienda no hay educación” en distintos institutos de la Comunidad de Madrid con el fin de que las familias y alumnado que tuviesen una situación de vivienda precaria o se fuesen a enfrentar a un desahucio supiesen cómo actuar y pudiésemos atajarlo no solo desde el sindicato sino también desde los centros educativos. 




Lo que refleja esta situación es que la socialdemocracia supeditada al neoliberalismo no está garantizando que los trabajadores tengan sus necesidades básicas cubiertas y este hecho está provocando una oleada de protestas y huelgas en toda Europa. España no es una excepción.. El maltrato de los servicios públicos, como educación o sanidad, y la mala gestión del problema de la vivienda en España están siendo el talón de Aquiles del “gobierno más progresista de la historia”.




¿Qué logros han obtenido ya gracias a la huelga y qué lecciones están surgiendo a medida que esta avanza?




En el momento en el que se hace esta entrevista, la consejera de educación de la Comunidad de Madrid se sigue negando a negociar con el comité de huelga. Llevamos ya más de dos semanas de huelga. 




Pero sabemos que hemos conseguido dotar de fuerza a las trabajadoras para luchar por una mejora en sus condiciones laborales. Hemos conseguido devolver el foco a las aulas y mostrar cuál es la realidad de la educación pública, mostrando que el gobierno de la Comunidad de Madrid no tiene ninguna intención de sostenerla. Hemos conseguido organizarnos y vamos a conseguir ganar. Esto no para.

author: Carlos Pérez
title: ‘This Isn’t Stopping’: A Rank-And-File Perspective on the Indefinite Strike for Public Education in Madrid
content:
Since October 14, teachers in Madrid, Spain, have been on an indefinite strike in defense of public education. After years of deteriorating conditions and systematic rank-and-file organizing, teachers have flooded the streets of Spain’s capital in a mass mobilization that has linked the fight for public education with the recent revolt around housing. 




The shared struggle for housing and public education in Spain is now heading toward a general strike on November 11 in the midst of a broader uprising spreading throughout Europe. 




Carlos Pérez, a North Carolina high school social studies teacher and Labor Notes board member, spoke with María, a secondary school teacher of history and geography in Madrid and a member of 

Menos Lectivas

 (a group whose name means “Fewer Teaching Hours”), one of the leading rank-and-file forces behind the strike. 




Pérez: Public school teachers in Madrid have been on an indefinite strike since October 14. What are the main issues that drove you and other teachers to call for a strike and what are your demands?




María:

 In the Community of Madrid, we have been dealing with cuts to public education since 2011. These have led to the deterioration of classroom conditions and the quality of education for students in the region.




A lack of resources and staff, high student-to-teacher ratios, an increase in direct teaching hours, and a failure to maintain or build necessary infrastructure have created a situation where teaching has become extremely difficult. We, as educators, are unable to adequately attend to all our students, and we have decided to take a stand against the institutional mistreatment that both we and our students are subjected to. 




In my case, I’ve taught high school classes with 33 students; I had to find a classroom to accommodate my students every day for a month of heavy rain because the classrooms had leaks that kept them constantly wet; my students with special educational needs (autism or hearing and speech difficulties) were not supported by the necessary professionals because there was neither a social integration specialist nor a teacher specifically assigned to them; and of course, I work an enormous amount of unpaid and unrecognized overtime.




This is why we are demanding that the Community of Madrid reduce the number of instructional hours; lower the teacher-to-student ratios; end segregation, given that the Community of Madrid is the most segregated region in Spain in terms of education; increase salaries to bring them in line with current economic needs; and reduce bureaucracy, among other things.




Menos Lectivas

, a rank-and-file formation that includes several unions, has been a driving force behind the strike. What is Menos Lectivas and what role has it played in the strike?




Menos Lectivas

 was founded in 2023, inspired by groups like Labor Notes in the United States, with the goal of organizing education workers from within their workplaces and returning union power to the workers themselves. Since then, we have built our movement through assemblies held at individual workplaces.




In the years leading up to the indefinite strike, we organized strikes, demonstrations, and rallies. These actions helped the movement grow and, crucially, provided us with the institutional legitimacy—both with the workers, who view us as a legitimate force for struggle because they feel part of it through our assemblies, and with other unions, the media, and ultimately the government—to decide how, when, and where we would fight for the right to education and for our own labor rights.




From the outset, we knew that an indefinite strike would be our ultimate tool for union struggle if our demands went unheeded by the Community of Madrid. Last June, it was decided in an assembly that we, the teachers, would launch an indefinite strike.




Given that these assemblies held clear legitimacy, the other unions that were not part of 

Menos Lectivas

 had no choice but to sit down with us on the Strike Committee to negotiate the establishment of a formal negotiating table and the terms of the strike.. This milestone is already a success; it has shifted power back into the hands of the workers, taking it out of the administrative offices.




How has the strike been received by students and their families?




Both families and students support our demands. Ultimately, they are the primary beneficiaries of the improvements we achieve. We feel very well supported by them, and they are an essential part of the struggle.




Organized students have also called for an indefinite strike, acting through various political parties and organizations such as the 

Sindicato de Estudiantes

 (Students’ Union) and the 

Organización Estudiantil Socialista

 (Socialist Student Organization). They are present at all our street actions and play a significant role in the struggle for education.




Families, meanwhile, are organizing themselves into associations, both within individual educational institutions and across neighborhoods, and are helping to support strike funds. They have also organized a demonstration of their own to show the Minister of Education that this struggle is not limited to teachers, but also involves families.




Given that the strike is indefinite, what kind of tactics have you all used to maintain collective participation and pressure?




We are constantly out in the streets—holding rallies, demonstrations, performances, and assemblies—occupying enough space to ensure that the media takes note of our demands.




It is important for the public to see and hear us, so that they become aware of the reality inside our classrooms. Once they are aware of it, they join the struggle, as I mentioned with students and their families..




This strike is taking place under the progressive government of Pedro Sanchez from the Spanish Socialist Workers Party (

Partido Socialista Obrero Español

, PSOE). How has Sánchez’s government responded to the strike?




On October 5, the Prime Minister called for general elections in Spain, meaning this strike has now become part of an electoral campaign. They had no choice but to express their support for the teachers in Madrid.




However, throughout the eight years that the PSOE has been in power in Spain, they have done nothing to improve conditions for either teaching staff or students. The government washes its hands of the matter, arguing that jurisdiction over education lies with the Autonomous Communities; yet, the Ministry of Education and the central government remain responsible for both the working conditions of staff and the education of all Spaniards.




Also, the Government Delegation—which is part of and directed by the central government, and which oversees the National Police—has offered no explanation for the brutal police crackdowns that both teachers and students have endured during the demonstrations and rallies held over the past month.




The strike in public education is taking place during a mass uprising around housing in and beyond Madrid. To what extent have these two struggles been linked?




Menos Lectivas

 has always maintained a close relationship with the Madrid Tenants’ Union (

Sindicato de Inquilinas de Madrid

). A year ago, a shared plan titled “No Housing, No Education” was launched in various secondary schools across the Community of Madrid. Its purpose was to ensure that families and students facing precarious housing situations or the threat of eviction would know how to respond, allowing us to address these issues not only through the union but also in our schools.




This situation reveals that social democracy, subordinated to neoliberalism, is failing to ensure that workers’ basic needs are met, which is fueling a wave of protests and strikes across Europe. Spain is no exception.. The neglect of public services, such as education and health care, combined with the mismanagement of the housing crisis in Spain, has become the Achilles' heel of what has been described as the “most progressive government in history.”




What gains have you already seen from the strike and what lessons are already emerging as the strike advances?




At the time of this interview, the Madrid regional government’s Minister of Education continues to refuse to negotiate with the strike committee. We are now more than two weeks into the strike.




Yet, we know that we have succeeded in giving strength to the workers in their fight for better working conditions. We have managed to shift the focus back to the classrooms and reveal the reality of public education, demonstrating that the Madrid regional government has no intention of supporting education. We have succeeded in organizing ourselves and we are going to win. This isn’t stopping.

author: Ellen David Friedman
title: Steward’s Corner: Rethink the Scripted ‘Ask’
content:
You’re having a conversation with a co-worker, but inside you’re feeling icy dread. You’re talking through a script that ends with asking them to do a specific thing: sign a union card, wear a button, come to a meeting, vote for a strike. And sure enough, when you ask, a wall comes down.




The co-worker looks away, makes an excuse, and pins you as someone who is after something. You’re disappointed, confused about why it didn’t work, and afraid you’re not going to meet your goal.




Many of us feel nervous or awkward about asking a co-worker to do something. Sometimes we just need to push ourselves to do it. But if you’re being pressured to follow the script and get to a particular “ask” without finding out who this person is and moving at their pace, that’s a problem.




A co-worker you don’t yet have much of a relationship with may be turned off that you’re pressuring them to take an action that has already been decided on by others.




What can you do instead? Replace the “ask” (to take some predetermined action) with an invitation: “Hey, some of us are getting together to talk about this. You want to join us?” “Can we figure out how you can be part of the solution to this problem that you’re posing?”




People are happy to be asked to do something they want to do, or that they’re good at, or that they’re confident about. People like to be asked to do things when it re

author: Luis Fernando Mora Reyes
title: Cómo construimos nuestro programa de educación sindical
content:
A principios de este año, surgió un debate entre miembros de nuestro sindicato, la Unión Nacional de Trabajadores por Aplicación (UNTA), a raíz de un comunicado en redes sociales que condenaba el secuestro por parte de los Estados Unidos, del presidente venezolano Nicolás Maduro y que exigía: “la defensa de la soberanía, la autodeterminación de los pueblos y la paz en América Latina”. 




Entre las bases del sindicato hubo posicionamientos encontrados sobre el comunicado, lo que generó que en la consiguiente Asamblea Coordinadora (en este espacio se informa, se discute y se llega a acuerdos entre las representaciones nacionales y locales del sindicato) se discutiera abiertamente sobre el tema. Hubo fuertes discusiones en las que existieron puntos de vista opuestos. Sin embargo, siempre se extendieron las opiniones con respeto y camaradería. 




Desde el sindicato entendimos que era necesario contar con espacios de discusión y análisis que permitieran mejorar nuestras capacidades políticas y sindicales.  Como resultado, los miembros decidieron constituir el Consejo Político Nacional (CPN), un espacio dentro del sindicato para el debate y las capacitaciones sobre temas políticos, económicos, laborales, de género y de cuestiones sociales. 




De esta forma, la Secretaría de Formación y Cultura propuso, en el marco del CPN, una serie de talleres de formación y capacitación política y sindical para todas las personas afiliadas. Los talleres buscaron resolver tres puntos: 







pensar de forma colectiva sobre temas de importancia nacional e internacional; 




fortalecer nuestras habilidades como afiliados del sindicato; 




fomentar una mayor participación en el día a día. 







El programa está conformado por cuatro grandes ejes en función de las necesidades del sindicato y se extendió la invitación tanto a las personas afiliadas como a especialistas a participar como ponentes en alguno de los temas. 




TEMAS DE PRIORIDAD




Los cuatro ejes son: 







talleres sobre el Convenio 193 de la OIT;




talleres sobre comprensión e interpretación de los Estatutos sindicales de la organización;




talleres sobre elementos técnicos para administrar los espacios sindicales; 




talleres de afiliación/organización.







Debido a que la UNTA formó parte de las discusiones sobre el Convenio 193 en materia de trabajo decente en la economía de plataformas en junio de este año, surgió la necesidad de que todas las personas afiliadas conocieran y comprendieran la relevancia de este. La necesidad de esto radica en que, desde el sindicato, se ha impulsado la ratificación del Convenio 193 en México y en el mundo, ya que, a partir de esto, podrán hacerse mejoras a la ley vigente en materia de trabajo por aplicación de México. 




Respecto a los tres ejes restantes del programa de capacitaciones, estos se encuentran íntimamente ligados entre sí. Una persona afiliada que conoce sus Estatutos puede participar activamente en cualquier área del sindicato. Asimismo, es necesario que los actuales representantes del sindicato profundicen en el conocimiento de los Estatutos. De igual manera, para prevenir malentendidos entre las personas afiliadas y los representantes, así como para profesionalizar los procesos internos de la organización, resulta fundamental que todas las personas afiliadas a la UNTA conozcan diversos elementos técnicos para administrar los espacios sindicales. Finalmente, para continuar construyendo poder colectivo, es crucial que los mismos afiliados se consideren organizadores—y podemos fomentar eso mediante talleres de afiliación y organización sindical. 




CONVERSACIONES VIRTUALES




Debido a cuán grande es el territorio mexicano, así como a la naturaleza del trabajo por aplicación, las capacitaciones se han llevado a cabo de manera virtual. Es decir, algunas personas se conectan desde el celular cuando están haciendo un servicio o toman tiempo de trabajo para continuar formándose y capacitándose. Esta es una clara muestra de la convicción que existe entre las personas afiliadas para continuar capacitándose y desarrollando sus habilidades. No obstante, para no intervenir ni interrumpir la jornada de trabajo con tanta frecuencia, los talleres se llevan a cabo cada tres semanas los días jueves. Hasta este momento, terminamos con el primer tema (el Convenio 193) e iniciamos con el segundo (comprensión de los Estatutos). Lo más importante es que todas las personas afiliadas a la UNTA contemos con espacios para la discusión y el análisis político, en donde la pluralidad de ideas sea el eje central y no un impedimento para continuar con la conversación. El que las personas afiliadas al sindicato tomen la decisión de conectarse para continuar formándose es una muestra del liderazgo y la convicción de las bases. 




Cabe destacar que, al interior de las capacitaciones, para guiar las discusiones, se dejan cuatro preguntas guía por tema. Al final, cada representación local debe entregar a la Secretaría de Formación y Cultura un escrito breve en el que se responden de manera puntual las preguntas. Con estos ejercicios se ha buscado incentivar la participación y discusión de las bases, fortalecer la habilidad de exposición de los ponentes, y fomentar en los afiliados un sentido de pertenencia y respeto a su sindicato. Por ejemplo, en cuanto al tema de la comprensión de los Estatutos, con las discusiones, las preguntas guía y los documentos escritos por las bases pueden comenzar a plantearse cambios, mejoras o adecuaciones a los mismos. Esto también se hizo durante los talleres del Convenio 193.




ABIERTOS AL DESACUERDO




A la UNTA siempre le ha preocupado la formación y capacitación constantes por parte de las bases y de los representantes. Entendemos la necesidad de tener conversaciones complejas que pueden llegar a ser incómodas políticamente, porque estar abierto a abordar los desacuerdos hace que el sindicato sea más fuerte. 




Sin espacios de discusión y análisis se frena el desarrollo de la organización. Somos partidarios de llevar a cabo conversaciones difíciles, pero bajo ciertas reglas que permitan el diálogo y la escucha activa. Por ejemplo, para pensar temas difíciles, hay que plantear preguntas incómodas. El no estar de acuerdo con un tema no quiere decir que seamos enemigos, sino que ilustra la necesidad de pensar en los sindicatos como espacios políticos de personas que tal vez no estén de acuerdo con todo, pero que luchan juntos por metas compartidas. 




Luis Fernando Mora Reyes es secretario de Formación y Cultura del CEN de la UNTA.

author: Luis Fernando Mora Reyes
title: How We Built Our Union’s Member Education Program
content:
Earlier this year, a debate broke out among members of our union, the National App Workers Union of Mexico (UNTA), after the union’s social media post condemning the U.S. government’s kidnapping of Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro and demanding “the defense of sovereignty, self determination and peace in Latin America.” 




Union members had conflicting views about the kidnapping, which led to a discussion on the subject in our next coordinating assembly—a space where we inform, discuss, and reach agreements between union representatives. Members disagreed intensely, but expressed their views with respect and camaraderie.


It made us realize that we needed more spaces like this for face-to-face discussion and analysis within the union, to help us develop a shared politics and grow as trade unionists. Out of these discussions, members decided to create the National Political Council (CPN), a space for debate and training on political, economic, labor, gender, and social issues.




Within this space, our office for training and culture proposed to offer a series of workshops, open to all members, meant to accomplish three things: 







help us think collectively about national and international issues




strengthen our skills as union members




generate greater discussion within the day-to-day life of the union.

author: Lisa Xu
title: Reform Candidate Says UFCW Rep Tailed Him for 300 Miles to Thwart Petition Effort
content:
In a union that has been headed by one family with no competitive elections since 1984, a group of grocery workers is organizing for change. But this week, they say, union staff who back the incumbent administration went to outrageous lengths in an attempt to make sure there’s no election this year either.




On Monday afternoon, Eric Marcuz, a veteran Northern California Safeway worker, stopped at the union office to pick up blank petitions to get on the ballot in the union’s upcoming election. Marcuz is running for president on the 

At What Cost

 slate in the 23,000-member United Food and Commercial Workers (UFCW) Local 8-Golden State, one of the largest locals in the union.




To get on the ballot, Marcuz and his slate-mates have to collect 443 petition signatures—2 percent of the local’s active members—in the next two weeks. If they don’t get enough signatures, no election will be held.




After Marcuz picked up the petitions from the local’s Roseville office, he got in his car to drive three hours south to Fresno, to start collecting signatures with another candidate on his slate at a Save Mart store there. (The local spans a 10-hour stretch from Bakersfield up to the Oregon border).

author: Dan DiMaggio
title: Book Review: A Model for U.S.-Mexico Cross-Border Solidarity
content:
Labor law reform in Mexico has opened up a major opportunity for workers fighting for genuine, independent unions. What can U.S. unions do to support our brothers and sisters there? And how can we build cross-border campaigns to confront our common employers?




Unions asking these questions will find valuable ideas in the e-book 

International Solidarity in Action: The Relationship Between the United Electrical Workers (UE) and Frente Auténtico del Trabajo (FAT)

, available for free download 

here

. 




Author Robin Alexander, retired director of international affairs for UE, led her union’s partnership with the FAT, which began in 1992, during the campaign to oppose the North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA).




UE members were seeing their employers cut manufacturing jobs in the U.S. and shift production to Mexico. “The UE leadership became convinced that the union needed to find a labor organization it could work with in Mexico,” Alexander writes, “and also that it was essential to connect international work more directly with UE members and with organizing.”




In a meeting in Mexico to discuss the campaign against NAFTA, the UE found the FAT—the only Mexican labor organization to oppose NAFTA.

author: Sarah Hughes
title: Members Alarmed by End-Run around Democracy at Buffalo Health Care Local
content:
Things had been tense for some time inside the leadership of Communications Workers (CWA) Local 1168, a 4,800-member health care union based near Buffalo, New York. Still, it was a high-functioning local with a busy calendar of events, stewards handling grievances, organizers pursuing leads, and leaders organizing at work.




So it was a surprise to members in June when their parent union, CWA, put the local into trusteeship, at the request of the local’s president and seven of the nineteen executive board members.




Trusteeship meant the union’s bylaws and elected leaders were suspended, and most of its work temporarily ground to a halt. The appointed Director of Organizing and Mobilizing Mary Nowocien and elected Vice President Patrick Weisansal II found themselves locked out of their group chats, email, and union hall, and facing an internal union prosecution.




A staffer of CWA District 1, Erin Spaulding, was assigned as trustee—tasked with maintaining the functioning of the local, setting up and overseeing judicial processes for the charges against officers, and making a plan to return the union to local control.




Nowocien and Weisansal saw the sudden trusteeship as an escalation of a long-running conflict and a deliberate undermining of the upcoming union elections. Weisansal had just announced his intention to run against incumbent President Cori Gambini.

author: Unknown
title: Bottom-Up Organizing: How We Got Clean Porta-Johns
content:
The first day I showed up on the Marriott construction site in downtown Detroit, everyone warned me about the state of our bathrooms. 




You could smell them halfway across most floors. They were full in 24 hours, urinals were often clogged, and some people had taken to using buckets and hiding them in closets. 




Every electrician already had the same idea: we wanted the cleaning schedule changed from twice a week to three times.




I had a long conversation with the steward about what had been tried. The first instinct of a construction worker is to “drag” (quit), drive over to the union hall, and pick up a new job. As expected, there was a steady trickle of drags, but no improvement to conditions.




OSHA had been called and walked the site, only to say that the number of bathrooms was up to their standard. The electrical contractor had been notified, but because the bathrooms were for all the trades, our bosses didn’t feel it was their responsibility to pay for additional cleaning. 




Our Electrical Workers (IBEW) Local 58 contract only gestures vaguely to “sanitary facilities,” and protects us explicitly should we leave the site to find a “sanitary” facility. This clause was exercised regularly, but no one could say for sure whether the boss was even aware we were leaving.

author: Kari Thompson
title: The First-Ever California State Workers’ Strike
content:
State workers went on a one-day unfair labor practice strike across California October 21, with picket lines in Sacramento, San Francisco, Los Angeles, and other cities. They're demanding better pay, affordable health care coverage, and flexibility to work from home. 




This was the first strike in the history of SEIU Local 1000, which represents about 100,000 government employees, ranging from accountants to custodians to nurses at state offices, hospitals, and prisons. 




They have been working without a contract since July 1. Some 5,000 employees were 

excluded

 from striking.




Governor Gavin Newsom’s “return-to-office” mandate went into effect this past summer. It requires workers to be in the office four days per week—even though workers report there isn’t enough space for all of them.




Workers argue the return-to-work policy compounds the lack of pay increases. Being forced back into the office is “more than just a pay cut,” said Jonah Paul, who works for the Employment Development Department in Sacramento. ”It’s a huge reduction in quality of life.




“Telework is a stopgap for a lot of problems our society is not willing to address,” Paul said: “the cost of childcare, and insane commutes. Telework becomes a catch-all solution for a grueling life.”

author: Lisa Xu
title: UFCW Members Protect Local Election After Sham Merger Attempt
content:
An insurgent slate is challenging the longtime incumbents in Local 8-Golden State, one of the largest locals in the United Food and Commercial Workers (UFCW), in what may be the local’s first competitive election in decades. And now, after protecting the election from a sham merger attempt that would have canceled the election, the battle is on. 




Ballots are set to be mailed on November 21. But when members first saw the election notice in the local’s newsletter, they discovered a big “but.” The notice stated that the election would not proceed if Local 8 merged with another union, the 

Staffing Agencies Federated Employees

 (SAFE), before the end of the year. 




Members said they had never heard about this possible merger, or SAFE, before reading about it in the final sentence of the election notice, mailed to members on October 16. 




What is SAFE? Publicly available information about the organization, which has multiple ties to Local 8 President Jacques Loveall, raised more questions than answers. Neither Local 8, the UFCW International union, nor SAFE has responded to inquiries about the merger.

author: Natascha Elena Uhlmann
title: Mexico Volkswagen Workers Could Soon Strike
content:
In Mexico, at the world’s largest Volkswagen facility outside of Germany, workers are weighing the risks of a possible strike.




The 6,500 workers build the Jetta, Tiguan, and Taos at the company’s Puebla plant. Their union, SITIAVW, is one of Mexico’s most storied independent unions, and is in the midst of the plant’s annual wage reopener negotiations.




Days before the strike deadline of October 22, the company presented two proposals—offering raises of 7.98 percent and 7.95 percent for a one-year duration—which were rejected by the union. Soon afterwards, the company presented another offer: an 8.24 percent increase, of which 3.59 percent is a one-time payment of 12,000 pesos, equivalent to about $641 U.S. The deal would maintain the yearly salary reopener, a cycle the company had tried to lengthen in previous offers. Workers will vote on the offer on October 28, and could strike the next day if a deal is not reached. 




On October 15, workers voted down an offer that  would have provided a 13 percent combined increase to wages and benefits over the next two years. The vote was 3,135 against and 2,452 for.
